_: The verb trainer's data. EMPTY ON PURPOSE - the verbs go in once there are
stories, because verbs.py refuses any verb the course does not teach.
kind: principal-parts. NOT the Spanish shape, and the reasoning is written
out over verbPartItems() in the app's engine.js. The short version: three of
German's five useful tenses are two words with the rest of the clause
between them, so a four-button card cannot hold them without lying about
word order. Principal parts fit on a card and are the thing no rule reaches.
EVERY FIELD IS STATED. Nothing here may be produced by a rule. Ablaut has
no rule, and a plausible guess - er sprecht, er fahrt, er nehmt - is exactly
the mistake the learner already makes. Handing it back as the right answer
is worse than having no trainer at all. es-ni paid for this once: its tables
turned estar into esto and taught cerro and perdo for years.
One entry, in full:
"sprechen": {
"en":    "to speak",      gloss, first sense only
"pres3": "spricht",       er/sie/es, present
"pres2": "sprichst",      du, present
"past3": "sprach",        er/sie/es, Praeteritum
"pp":    "gesprochen",    participle
"aux":   "hat",           hat or ist, nothing else
"imp":   "sprich",        du imperative        (optional)
"pre":   null,            the prefix, if it has one   (optional)
"sep":   false,           does that prefix come off?  (optional)
"k2":    "spraeche"       Konjunktiv II, only where it lives (optional)
pre and sep travel together and both are needed for the prefix question.
umsteigen is pre um / sep true and its pres3 is written SEPARATED,
"steigt um". umarmen is pre um / sep false and its pres3 is "umarmt".
Asking the question of both is the point: if it only ran on separable verbs
the answer would always be the split one and the card could be played
without reading it.
drill: which verbs the trainer draws from. Leave it empty and it draws from
every entry. Use it to hold a verb back rather than deleting it.
Checked by .github/scripts/verbs.py, which stage.py runs every time.

kennen.en: to know a person or place
